common_name: Variegatum Bigroot Geranium (Cream-Streaked Fragrant Groundcover Cranesbill)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in average to rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this rarely offered bigroot selection is slower and less vigorous than the plain green species.

directions: This selection of bigroot geranium carries the same aromatic, musky-scented foliage and small magenta-pink early-summer flowers as the species, but each leaf is softly streaked and edged in creamy yellow rather than solid green. Grow it in a woodland setting with protection from hot afternoon sun, since the variegation can scorch in full exposure and fades in deep shade. Watch new growth for occasional all-green reversion shoots and cut these out promptly, as they grow faster than the variegated portions and will eventually overtake the clump. It spreads more slowly than ordinary macrorrhizum, making it a well-behaved choice for edging shaded paths or underplanting shrubs where a less aggressive groundcover is wanted.

common_name: Cedric Morris Bloody Cranesbill (Upright Vivid Magenta-Pink Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; named and introduced through the garden of British plantsman and painter Cedric Morris.

directions: Cedric Morris stands apart from typical bloody cranesbill by growing noticeably more upright and a little taller, rather than hugging the ground in the loose mound most sanguineum selections form. Its finely cut, palmately lobed leaves are topped through summer by a long succession of vivid magenta-pink flowers that hold their color well even in strong sun. It tolerates poor, dry soils once established and needs little more than an annual shearing after the first flush of bloom to stay tidy and encourage rebloom. Use it at the front of a sunny border, tucked among roses, or as a durable, low-care groundcover on a slope.

common_name: Margaret Wilson Mourning Widow Geranium (Cream-Marbled Foliage Dusky Cranesbill)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade to full sun; this variegated mourning widow selection colors best with some direct light.

directions: Margaret Wilson is grown as much for its foliage as for its flowers, each leaf emerging in spring with an irregular marbling of creamy white and light green that gradually settles to a subtler green flush as the season progresses. Nodding, dusky purple-violet flowers held on wiry stems rise above the foliage in mid-spring, in classic mourning widow fashion, but fade more quickly than the leaf color show that follows. Give it morning sun or filtered light rather than deep shade to keep the variegation bright, and consistently moist soil, since this phaeum selection is less drought-tolerant than the plain species. It makes an effective accent at the front of a shaded border or as a long-season filler in a woodland container.

common_name: Opalescence Garden Phlox (Dark-Eyed Light Pink Luminary Series Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock in spring in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil with full air circulation; a Proven Winners Luminary series introduction bred for powdery mildew resistance.

directions: Opalescence is the flagship of the Luminary series, bred primarily for its exceptional resistance to the powdery mildew that disfigures so many older tall garden phlox by midsummer. Light pink petals surround a noticeably darker pink eye, and the tightly formed, rounded flower panicles sit above clean, dark green foliage from midsummer into fall. Space plants generously and keep them well watered at the root zone rather than overhead to further discourage foliar disease, and deadhead spent panicles to extend bloom. It draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds in steady numbers and holds up well as a cut flower.

common_name: Ultraviolet Garden Phlox (Dark Magenta-Violet Luminary Series Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock in spring in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil with full sun and open air circulation; a Proven Winners Luminary series introduction.

directions: Ultraviolet brings the deepest, most saturated color in the Luminary lineup, with dense panicles of dark magenta-violet flowers held well above bright green, mildew-resistant foliage. It is the tallest of the series and benefits from a sheltered spot or light staking in windy gardens to keep the sturdy stems upright through the long summer-to-fall bloom season. Full sun brings out the richest flower color and keeps growth compact and dense, while consistently moist soil and good spacing between plants help it shrug off the fungal leaf spot that plagues older garden phlox varieties. It is a strong magnet for bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds and performs equally well in borders or as a cut flower.

common_name: Sunset Coral Garden Phlox (Light-Responsive Coral-Orange Luminary Series Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock in spring in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest flower color; a Proven Winners Luminary series introduction.

directions: Sunset Coral is unusual among garden phlox for how much its flower color shifts with light intensity, opening a soft coral pink in cooler or shadier conditions and deepening to a vivid coral-orange glow under strong, direct sun. The fragrant flowers form well-filled panicles over clean, mildew-resistant foliage from summer through fall, making this a long season of color even without deadheading. Grow it in full sun for the most dramatic color saturation and keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged, with good spacing for airflow. Its pollinator appeal and strong disease resistance have made it a widely recommended border and landscape selection.

common_name: Prismatic Pink Garden Phlox (Bubblegum Pink Dark-Eyed Luminary Series Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock in spring in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; a Proven Winners Luminary series introduction.

directions: Prismatic Pink carries large, densely packed panicles of bubblegum pink flowers, each marked with a contrasting dark pink eye that gives the whole flower head a lively, dotted look from a distance. The fragrance carries well in the garden and draws a steady stream of bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds through its long summer-to-fall bloom window. Site it in full sun with slightly acidic to neutral, evenly moist soil, and provide good air circulation between plants to take advantage of its improved mildew resistance compared to heirloom paniculata varieties. It performs equally well massed in a perennial border or cut for arrangements.

common_name: Backlight Garden Phlox (Pure White Dark-Foliage Luminary Series Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock in spring in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; a Proven Winners Luminary series introduction well suited to moonlight gardens.

directions: Backlight produces clean, pure white flowers in tight, well-formed panicles that stand out sharply against glossy dark green foliage, an effect that is especially striking at dusk or under evening light. It is more compact and narrower in habit than other members of the Luminary series, making it easier to tuck into smaller borders without crowding neighboring plants. Grow in full sun with consistently moist, well-drained soil and good spacing for airflow, since strong disease resistance is one of its main selling points over older white garden phlox. Pair it with other pale or silver-foliaged plants to anchor a white or moonlight-themed planting.

common_name: Pink Lightning Garden Phlox (Large-Flowered White-Starburst Luminary Series Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock in spring in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; a Proven Winners Luminary series introduction with the largest individual flowers in the series.

directions: Pink Lightning bears the largest individual florets of the Luminary series, each a bright true pink marked with a crisp white starburst radiating from the center, giving the whole panicle a sparkling, patterned look. Growers have reported its foliage staying essentially free of powdery mildew well into fall, a notable improvement over many older tall phlox cultivars. It flowers over an unusually long stretch from summer through fall and tolerates brief dry spells better than most garden phlox once established, though regular watering keeps bloom quality highest. Grow in full sun with good air circulation and deadhead spent panicles to encourage continued flowering for bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds.

common_name: Fran's Purple Creeping Phlox (Top-Rated Purple-Lilac Woodland Groundcover Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; rated the top-performing creeping phlox selection in a multi-year Mt. Cuba Center trial.

directions: Fran's Purple forms a dense, fast-spreading mat of small evergreen leaves that stays slightly lower and tighter than the popular Sherwood Purple selection, with abundant rich purple-lilac flowers covering the foliage in spring. It earned the top overall performance rating in a multi-year regional trial of creeping phlox selections, outscoring most other named cultivars for vigor, flower coverage, and foliage quality. Grow it in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in a woodland setting with partial to full shade, where it spreads readily by surface stolons to knit together as a durable, weed-suppressing groundcover. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat tidy and encourage dense new growth for the following season.
